office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Griffith Public Schools serves most of the town of Griffith in Lake County [24]. The district reports 1,995 students in three schools: Wadsworth Elementary (mainly grades PK–2), Beiriger Elementary (mainly grades 3–5) and Griffith Jr/Sr High School (grades 6–12) [25]. Leah Dumezich is superintendent [26, 27].

The board has five members, all elected at large [26]. Its 2026 officers are President Emily Conner, 1st Vice President Jesse Adduci, 2nd Vice President Tina Adams, Secretary Kathy Ruesken and Assistant Secretary Jason Jaques [28, 27].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: three at-large seats. The county's sample ballot says 'Vote for not more than Three (3)' [29]; the state list's 'vote for 1' understates the number of seats. The three terms ending Dec. 31, 2026 belong to Adams, Adduci and Ruesken [26]. Adams and Ruesken are running again; Adduci is not on the candidate list [30].

In 2022 the three at-large winners were Adams (1,995 votes), Jennifer Gooldy (1,816) and Ruesken (1,769); Adduci finished fourth with 1,410 [31]. The 2026 county directory lists Adduci in a seat whose term ends in 2026 [26]. This guide did not confirm how he joined the board.
Not on this ballot: Conner and Jaques won the two at-large seats on the 2024 ballot, and their terms run through 2028 [32, 26].

Candidates: Tina Adams, Lori A Rose and Kathy Ruesken are printed on the ballot, and Patrick Janke is a declared write-in candidate. That makes four candidates for three seats [30, 29]. The ballot says a write-in vote counts only if it is for a declared write-in candidate [29].

Operating referendum (2022): in May 2022 voters approved Griffith's operating referendum 1,309 to 796 [33]. It runs for eight years at a rate of $0.3294 and was projected to raise about $2.29 million a year, $2.08 million of it for retaining and attracting teachers and staff [34]. The district's website lists the staff salaries paid from referendum funds [25].

Budget (2025–2026): at the Oct. 9, 2025 meeting, which included the public hearing on the 2026 budget, Dumezich explained how the referendum and tax rate work and said the district 'will have to keep looking at reductions each year due to the tax rate' [35]. At the Sept. 10, 2026 meeting, Chief Financial Officer Terri Chance reported that the budget is down $1.6 million from circuit-breaker tax caps, which will affect transportation and maintenance. She said the 2027 budget hearing would be held in September and the budget adopted in October [27]. In July 2026 the board unanimously approved transfers from the Debt Service Fund and the Education Fund to the Operations Fund (Resolutions 2026-18 and 2026-19) [36]. The minutes this guide read do not quantify the effect of the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1).

Facilities (2025–2026): the Oct. 9, 2025 meeting also included a project hearing and a second preliminary determination hearing [35]. In January 2026 Dumezich gave target completion dates of June 5, 2026 for the indoor athletic facility, July 14 for the football, soccer and track fields, and July 31 for the varsity locker rooms. She said the aquatic center would be finished at the end of September, with a public opening hoped for in the second week of October 2026 [37].

Storm recovery (2026): an Aug. 11, 2026 storm delayed the start of school, and the district had about $170,000 in insurance claims as of Sept. 10 [27]. That month the board unanimously adopted resolutions declaring an emergency requiring mitigation and restoration, and authorizing pay for classified staff during unplanned emergency closures [27].

Other 2026 board items: the board unanimously kept the superintendent on a three-year contract in July 2026 [36]. In January 2026 Dumezich reported that 26 students were enrolled in the district's online Region Virtual Academy, with a goal of 50 by the end of the school year, and described it as a way to bring in revenue [37]. In September 2026 the board approved a peer tutoring course, a test security policy and an amended 2026–2027 strategic plan. Audience members that month questioned athletic pass prices and bus fees for fine arts trips [27].
Forums: this guide found no candidate forums, questionnaires or news coverage of the 2026 Griffith school board race.

candidates.summary: Incumbent; elected at large in 2022 and now board secretary [31, 28].
background: Has served on the board since winning an at-large seat in 2022 [31]. Was 1st vice president in 2025 and is secretary in 2026 [35, 28]. This guide found no information on her occupation.
path_to_ballot: Filed May 19, 2026 without a party affiliation; no party appears under her name on the ballot [30, 29, 6].
on_incumbent: Is a current board member. In September 2026 she moved to approve the new peer tutoring course, the emergency mitigation resolution and the amended strategic plan, all of which passed unanimously [27]. In January 2026 she moved to postpone the board's reorganization to February, when all members would be present [37].

candidates.summary: Incumbent; was the top vote-getter in the 2022 at-large race and was board president in 2025 [31, 35].
background: Won an at-large seat in 2022 as Tina G Adams, with the most votes in that race [31]. Was board president in 2025 and through the January 2026 meeting, and is 2nd vice president in 2026 [35, 37, 28]. This guide found no information on her occupation.
path_to_ballot: Filed May 19, 2026 as a Republican, and 'Republican Party' is printed under her name on the ballot [30, 29, 6]. In 2022 the county listed her as nonpartisan [31].

items: At the Oct. 9, 2025 meeting, during a discussion of athletic fees, the minutes record that she 'agrees that parents are responsible to pay the fees, but students need to learn accountability and that there are ways to fundraise' [35].
